parole.significato: barn (building, often found on a farm, used for storage or keeping animals such as cattle)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German stadel. Compare Czech stodola and German Stadel.

parole.significato: stack, pile, heap; a pile of identical objects
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German stoz, from Old High German stōz. Cognate with German Stoß. Doublet of sztos (“shot”).

parole.significato: to use, to apply, to employ [with w (+ locative) ‘at what’]
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish stosować.
Borrowed from Middle High German schrage. Doublet of szaragi.
Inherited from Old Polish strych, from Middle High German esterîch, esterich, estrich, from Medieval Latin astracus, astricus, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon).

Inherited from Old Polish strych, from Middle High German strich, from Old High German strih, from Proto-West Germanic *striki, from Proto-Germanic *strikiz, from Proto-Indo-European *strig-ís, from the root *streyg- (“to stroke”).

parole.significato: to injure pasterns by catching one leg with the other
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish strychować, from Middle High German strīchen, from Old High German strīhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *strīkan.

parole.significato: shah (king of Persia or Iran, or supreme ruler in some Middle Eastern or South Asian nations)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish szach. Doublet of czek.
Borrowed from Middle High German schaffaere. By surface analysis, szafować + -arz.

parole.significato: to jerk, tug, yank (pull something hard or suddenly)
parole.testo: Perhaps borrowed from Middle High German scharben.
Borrowed from Middle High German studel, stuodel.
Borrowed from Middle High German schopz, schöpz (“castrated male sheep”), from a West Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *skopьcь (“eunuch, someone castrated”). Doublet of skopiec.
Inherited from Old Polish szkoła. Doublet of schola.

parole.significato: nobility, gentry (noble or privileged social class)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish ślachta, ślechta, from Middle High German slahte, from Old High German slahta, from Proto-Germanic *slahtō. Compare German Geschlecht, Italian schiatta.
Borrowed from Middle High German slac.

From influence of Middle High German slucken (“to swallow, gobble, sob, snivel”) and slūchen (“to swallow, gobble”). Compare German schluchzen (“to sob”) which is derived from the frequentative/iterative form of Middle High German nouns.
Borrowed from Middle High German schopf(e), from Proto-Germanic *skup-.
Perhaps borrowed from Middle High German spaz /spatze (see modern German Spatz). Compare Belarusian шпак (špak), Czech špaček, Russian шпак (špak), and Ukrainian шпак (špak).
Inherited from Old Polish szpital. Doublet of hostel and hotel.
Inherited from Old Polish szram, *szrama, from Middle High German schramm, schramme.

parole.significato: art (conscious production or arrangement of sounds, colours, forms, movements, or other elements in a manner that affec…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish sztuka. Sense 1 was derived from sense 12. Doublet of stiuk.
Probably from szturać, from Middle High German stürn.

Inherited from Old Polish sturm, szturm, from Middle High German sturm, from Old High German sturm, from Proto-West Germanic *sturm, from Proto-Germanic *sturmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH-. Doublet of sztorm.
Borrowed from Middle High German stīf or Middle Low German stīf + -ny, from Proto-Germanic *stīfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *steypós.
Borrowed from Middle High German schūbe.

parole.significato: shift (change of workers); also the people of such a shift
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish szychta, from Middle High German schiht, from Middle Low German schicht.
Borrowed from Middle High German teller /teler /telier; see modern German Teller for more.
Borrowed from Middle High German tam(m).
Borrowed from Middle High German tanzer, tenzer.

parole.significato: dance (a sequence of rhythmic steps or movements usually performed to music, for pleasure or as a form of social intera…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish taniec, borrowed from Middle High German tanz, borrowed from Old French dance, danse. Compare Russian та́нец (tánec), German Tanz, Kashubian tuńc, Silesian taniec. Possibly cognate to Old High German dansōn (“to pull”).

Inherited from Old Polish tarcza, from Middle High German tartsche, from Old French targe, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *targǭ (“edge, rim”). Displaced Old Polish paweza and szczyt. Sense 5 coined by Jan Śniadecki.
Borrowed from Middle High German tragære.

Perhaps from trach + -ka, from Middle High German trache, tracke, drache, dracke, from Old High German trahho, from Proto-West Germanic *drakō, from Latin dracō, from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn). Doublet of Drakula.
Inherited from Old Polish trafta, trawta, tryfta, from Middle High German trift, from Proto-Germanic *driftiz. Doublet of dryf (“drift, leeway”).

parole.significato: tourney, tournament (during the Middle Ages, a series of battles and other contests designed to prepare knights for war)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German turnei, from Old French tourneoi, from Old French tornoiier.
Borrowed from Middle High German tūs, dūs (“deuce”) (German Daus), from Old French dous (“two”).
Borrowed from Middle High German wahte, from Old High German wahta, from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō (“watch, vigil”).

Possibly borrowed from Middle High German wahtære, from Old High German wahtāri. By surface analysis, wachta + -arz. Compare Russian вахтёр (vaxtjór), Silesian wachtyrz and Ukrainian вахте́р (vaxtér).

parole.significato: scale (device to measure mass or weight)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish waga.
Borrowed from Middle High German warte, from Old High German warta, from Proto-West Germanic *wardu.

parole.significato: condition (factor that must be met for something to happen)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish warunek. Compare German Wahrung.

parole.significato: open four-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle without springs or on transverse half-springs
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish wasąg, from Middle High German vazzunge. Doublet of fasunek.
Borrowed from Middle High German wal, from Latin vallum.

parole.significato: to wander aimlessly from place to place
parole.testo: From German faulenzen + -ać, from Middle High German vūlezen.

parole.significato: compensation (something which is regarded as an equivalent; something which compensates for loss)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish wet.

parole.significato: vetch (any plant of the genus Vicia)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish wyka, wika, attested from the 15th century, from Middle High German wicke, from Old High German wicka, from Latin vicia.
Etymology 2 sense 1 is a semantic loan from Middle High German sloȥ (cf. German Schloss) via Czech zámek, itself a semantic loan of Latin clūsa.
Inherited from Old Polish zradzić. By surface analysis, z- + radzić. Calque of Middle High German verrāten. For the epenthetic d, compare zdumieć, zdrój.

parole.significato: clock (chronometer, an instrument that measures time, particularly the time of day)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Polish zeger, borrowed from Middle High German seigære (“scales, clock”), from seigen. Compare German Seiger, Hungarian cseger, and Yiddish זייגער (zeyger). Compare also German Zeiger, which is etymologically unrelated but may have contributed to the semantic development.
Inherited from Old Polish żemła, from Middle High German semele, from Old High German semala, from Latin simila, of Semitic origin. Compare Silesian żymła.
Borrowed from Middle High German sidel, from Latin sedīle.
Borrowed from Middle High German zwicken, from Old High German *zwicchēn. Cognate with German zwicken, English twitch.

parole.significato: load, cargo, freight, charge (goods that are transported somewhere using special vehicles or other means designed for t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German ladunge. First attested in 1563. By surface analysis, ładować + -unek. Compare Kashubian ladënk and Silesian ladōnek /ladōng.

parole.significato: batten (horizontal wood beam supporting the tiles or other outer roofing material)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German latte /late.
Inherited from Old Polish łotr.
Borrowed from Middle High German louge, from Old High German louga, from Proto-West Germanic *laugu, from Proto-Germanic *laugō.
Inherited from Old Polish ścirciałka. Further etymology uncertain, perhaps from Middle High German schîrschalke.
Borrowed from Middle High German sloʒʒer. Compare German Schlosser.
Borrowed from Middle High German schrūbe. Further origin uncertain, compare German Schraube, Dutch schroef, English screw.

parole.significato: sail (piece of fabric attached to a boat and arranged such that it causes the wind to drive the boat along; it may be a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German sëgel.

parole.significato: to bid farewell, to bid goodbye
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German segenen, from Latin signō (whence also Czech žehnat, German segnen, English sain).
Inherited from Old Polish żołnierz.
Borrowed from Middle High German sūr. Doublet of ser.
